name: Equatoguinean Succotash
description: Succotash is genuinely the national dish of Equatorial Guinea, its real journey tracing back to Native American cooking, carried to the American South, and brought back to Africa by freed slaves and their descendants - real Equatoguinean versions are traditionally made without meat, built on real thyme, olive oil, and a splash of red wine vinegar for brightness.
steps_detailed: Cook the onion and garlic in the olive oil, 3-4 minutes.
Add the lima beans, corn, tomatoes, and thyme, and simmer 15-18 minutes until the beans are tender.
Stir in the vinegar just before serving for real brightness - traditionally made without meat.

name: Equatoguinean Pepesup
description: Pepesup (pepper soup), Equatorial Guinea's real signature dish given the country's deep fishing tradition, is a genuinely spicy fish soup built with real cassava leaves, used directly here since they're genuinely available frozen through African and Caribbean grocers in the US.
steps_detailed: Simmer the tomatoes, garlic, and jalapeño together, being generous with the pepper, 8-10 minutes.
Add the fish and cassava leaves, and simmer 12-15 minutes until the fish is just cooked through and the leaves are tender.

name: Equatoguinean Tortilla de Camarones
description: Tortilla de camarones, a shrimp omelet, genuinely reflects Equatorial Guinea's real Spanish colonial heritage as Central Africa's only Spanish-speaking nation - real technique cooks the eggs slowly over low heat, Spanish tortilla-style, rather than quickly scrambled.
steps_detailed: Cook the onion in the olive oil, 3-4 minutes, then add the shrimp and cook 2-3 minutes until just pink.
Pour in the beaten eggs and cook over low heat, undisturbed, 4-5 minutes, Spanish tortilla-style, until mostly set.
Flip carefully and cook 2-3 minutes more until fully set.

name: Equatoguinean Grilled Fish
description: Grilled fish rubbed with garlic and chili, reflecting Equatorial Guinea's rich Gulf of Guinea fishing tradition.
steps_detailed: Rub the fish with the garlic and jalapeño, and let sit 10 minutes.
Grill or broil, 4-5 minutes per side, until just cooked through.

name: Equatoguinean Peanut Chicken
description: Chicken with real peanut sauce is a beloved everyday Equatoguinean dish, real technique whisking the peanut butter slowly for a smooth sauce.
steps_detailed: Brown the chicken, 6-7 minutes.
Whisk the peanut butter slowly with the tomatoes and a little water, add to the pot.
Simmer 20-22 minutes until the chicken is tender.

name: Equatoguinean Fufu
description: Fufu, pounded cassava or yam, is a genuine Equatoguinean staple, traditionally paired with pepesup or other soups.
steps_detailed: Boil the cassava until completely soft, 20-25 minutes.
Drain and pound vigorously until smooth and stretchy, free of lumps.

name: Equatoguinean Fried Plantain
description: Fried ripe plantain, a common Equatoguinean side dish, real versions using genuinely ripe plantain for real caramelization.
steps_detailed: Fry the plantain slices in a little oil, turning once, 3-4 minutes per side, until deeply caramelized and golden.

name: Equatoguinean Bollería-Style Pastry
description: Bollería, Spanish-style pastries, reflect genuine Spanish colonial influence, real versions traditionally paired with café con leche for breakfast.
steps_detailed: Mix the flour, butter, sugar, and egg into a soft dough.
Shape into small rolls and bake at 375F (190C) for 15-18 minutes until golden.

Simmer 12-15 minutes until thickened.
